content: The effectiveness of vaccines can be assessed using test-negative, case-control studies. These studies are frequently conducted in the context of diarrhea or rotavirus surveillance. In such studies, confirmed cases of rotavirus gastroenteritis are designated as the cases, while confirmed cases of rotavirus-negative gastroenteritis serve as the controls. This study design is feasible due to the high specificity of the rotavirus enzyme immunoassay (EIA) test. It minimizes selection bias because all children are enrolled prospectively before their rotavirus infection status or vaccination status is confirmed. However, significant effort is required to accurately document the vaccination status of the enrolled children. To evaluate surveillance performance, specific attributes, indicators, targets, and calculation formulas are outlined. The ideal scenario is 12 months of reporting, with confirmed zero reporting if no cases are detected. Other indicators include the proportion of eligible cases enrolled, the number of suspected diarrhea cases reported annually, the timeliness of specimen collection (within two days of admission), and the proportion of specimens tested for rotavirus using EIA. The ideal targets for these indicators are generally set at 80–90%. Public health interventions to reduce diarrhea in communities emphasize improving hygiene, water supply, and wastewater disposal. Routine immunization of infants with rotavirus vaccines is now considered the most effective public health intervention for controlling rotavirus on a population-wide scale. Rotavirus is an RNA virus with seven known groups (A to G), of which group A is responsible for most human illnesses. The virus is classified into G and P genotypes, with G1P[8], G2P[4], G3P[8], G4P[8], G9P[8], and G12 (in combination with P[6] or P[8]) accounting for 90% of human infections. Rotavirus primarily affects infants aged 3 months to 1 year and is the leading cause of severe diarrheal disease in young children worldwide. The high mortality rate in less developed countries is attributed to limited access to timely healthcare, compounded by factors such as malnutrition, concurrent infections, and year-round transmission due to climatic conditions. In high-income countries, rotavirus accounted for 40–50% of hospital admissions for diarrheal disease in the pre-vaccine era. Rotavirus is highly communicable, with transmission occurring primarily via the fecal-oral route through close person-to-person contact or indirectly via contaminated surfaces (fomites). Transmission through contaminated water or food is uncommon. The infectious dose is very low, requiring fewer than 100 virus particles. The incubation period is short, typically less than 48 hours, and the illness usually lasts 3–7 days, though it can persist for 2–3 weeks in some cases. The disease is communicable from two days before the onset of diarrhea to several days after symptoms begin, during the acute phase and while virus shedding continues. Currently available rotavirus vaccines are live, oral, attenuated strains of human and/or animal origin that replicate in the human intestine to elicit an immune response. The World Health Organization (WHO) has prequalified four vaccines: Rotarix, RotaTeq, Rotavac, and Rotasiil. These vaccines have demonstrated good safety profiles. While an earlier vaccine, RotaShield, was associated with an increased risk of intussusception, recent randomized controlled trials of the four WHO-prequalified vaccines have shown no increased risk of intussusception after any dose. In 2016, rotavirus infection was estimated to cause 128,500 deaths globally among children under five years of age, with 37,765 of these deaths occurring in the WHO South-East Asia Region. The disease burden is higher in low-income countries due to factors such as malnutrition, concurrent infections, and limited access to healthcare. The WHO launched the Global Rotavirus Surveillance Network in 2008 to generate local data for decision-making on vaccine introduction, monitor disease trends and genotype distribution, and assess vaccine effectiveness. Surveillance officers at sentinel sites are responsible for daily ward surveys to identify eligible children, enrolling patients, collecting specimens, and ensuring timely laboratory testing. They must also maintain data logs, validate data, and share results with stakeholders. Regular monitoring of data quality is essential to identify issues in patient enrollment, specimen collection, and testing procedures. For example, if fewer than 75% of expected cases are enrolled for two consecutive months, it may indicate inadequate case-finding procedures. Similarly, if fewer than 15% of enrolled children test positive for rotavirus, the quality of stool specimens or testing procedures should be reviewed. Vaccination data should be sourced from vaccination cards, medical records, or maternal recall. Stool specimens are the primary sample type for testing, and enzyme immunoassay (EIA) is the most commonly used methodology.
